body_text:
Let $\Gamma$ be a collection of sentences and let $\varphi$ be a
sentence in a common formal language. We say that $\varphi$ is
a *semantic consequence* of $\Gamma$, written $\Gamma \models
\varphi$, if every interpretation (model) in which every
sentence of $\Gamma$ evaluates to true also makes $\varphi$
true.

Semantic consequence asserts that it is impossible for the
premises to be simultaneously true while the conclusion is
false. If no interpretation can satisfy all sentences in
$\Gamma$ simultaneously—that is, if $\Gamma$ is inconsistent—the
condition holds vacuously, and every sentence $\varphi$ in the
language is a semantic consequence of $\Gamma$. This phenomenon
is known classically as *ex falso quodlibet* (from a
contradiction, anything follows).
